title: Batching tiers (Fast / Standard / Cost-efficient) — Customer FAQ (DRAFT)
content:
DRAFT — Customer-facing FAQ for batching tiers.

Owner: Soojin (Product Messaging)
Last pass reviewers: Aditya (Optimize), Nikhil (Hosted API), Sean/Allison (SRE/Obs), Alex/Monica (DevEx)

Notes / intent
- This is meant to be copy we can adapt for docs + beta comms.
- Keep it practical: “which tier should I choose?”, “what happens to streaming?”, “when do I override?”
- Avoid promising exact latency numbers in this FAQ (those live in tier contracts / region+model specifics). Use relative guidance.
- TODO: confirm tier naming consistency: “cost-efficient” vs “eco” (current decision: “cost-efficient”).

---

FAQ

1) What are “batching tiers”?
Batching tiers are recommended, safe-by-default performance profiles that control how Redwood forms GPU batches and how long requests can wait in the queue before execution. They help you pick a predictable trade-off between:
- latency (including time-to-first-token)
- streaming cadence (how smooth tokens arrive)
- throughput (tokens/sec per GPU)
- cost per token

Instead of manually tuning low-level knobs (e.g., max batch size, queue delay, scheduler weights), you choose a tier:
- fast
- standard
- cost-efficient

Redwood selects sensible defaults per model family and hardware (and may apply minor workload-aware adjustments based on prompt length + concurrency).

2) Why did Redwood add tiers instead of “one best default”?
There isn’t one best batching configuration for every application. Example:
- A real-time chat experience cares about responsiveness and steady streaming.
- A background summarization pipeline cares more about $/token and throughput.
- A mixed workload needs a balanced baseline.

Tiers let you choose a stable contract while Redwood improves the underlying engine and model-specific tuning over time.

3) What’s the difference between fast, standard, and cost-efficient?
High level:
- fast: prioritizes user-perceived latency. Lower queue delay, lower batching aggressiveness, higher priority on decode responsiveness.
- standard: balanced baseline for most interactive + API workloads.
- cost-efficient: prioritizes throughput and $/token by allowing more batching and (typically) slightly higher queue delay. Best for async, batch, or high-concurrency workloads.

What changes under the hood (simplified):
- max_queue_delay_ms: how long Redwood may wait to build a batch
- max_batch_size / token budget: how large a batch can become
- prefill vs decode scheduling weights: how the scheduler prioritizes “starting” new requests vs “continuing” existing ones
- admission control / overload protection thresholds: when we start applying backpressure/load-shedding to protect tail latency and avoid error spikes

Important: Tier defaults can vary by model family and GPU SKU (because prefill cost, memory pressure, and optimal batch formation are different).

4) Which tier should I choose?
Rule of thumb:
- Choose fast if:
  - you have human-facing interactions (chat, copilots, support agents)
  - you stream responses to users
  - you care about time-to-first-token and “snappy” feel
- Choose standard if:
  - you want a default that works well across a broad mix
  - you have moderate streaming needs but also care about efficiency
  - you are unsure (start here)
- Choose cost-efficient if:
  - work is mostly async or batch (ETL, offline summarization, indexing)
  - your service can tolerate a bit more waiting to reduce cost
  - you run higher concurrency and want better GPU utilization

If you have different endpoints with different UX requirements, it’s common to pick different tiers per route.

5) How does tier selection impact streaming?
Streaming has two latency dimensions:
- time-to-first-token (TTFT): when the first token arrives
- token cadence: how consistent subsequent tokens arrive (avoiding “bursty” streaming)

In general:
- fast is designed to minimize TTFT and keep decode responsive so cadence is smooth.
- standard is usually fine for streaming, but TTFT may be slightly higher under load.
- cost-efficient may increase TTFT under load because it waits longer to form larger batches and prioritizes overall throughput.

If your product’s UX depends on very steady streaming (e.g., voice / realtime reading, live agent UI), we recommend fast. If you need streaming but it’s not strictly UX-critical, standard is typically the right default.

6) Will tiers change model output quality?
Batching tiers do not change model weights or sampling parameters directly. However, there are a few indirect effects:
- Different scheduling can change timing and cancellation patterns (especially for streaming clients that disconnect early).
- If you use tight client-side timeouts, more queue delay can cause more timeouts, which can look like “worse quality” (partial responses).

If you observe quality differences, check:
- timeout / cancellation rates
- whether your client disconnects before the model finishes
- whether your sampling settings differ across routes

Redwood also runs evaluation guardrails for batching changes to reduce the chance of regressions during rollouts.

7) What about function/tool calling and structured output?
For tool/function calling and structured output (JSON mode / constrained decoding), the main concern is reliability rather than speed.
- If you have strict server-side timeouts or tight UX loops (agent calling tools), pick fast or standard.
- cost-efficient can work well for background tool runs, but avoid it if you routinely operate near timeout thresholds.

8) Is cost-efficient “unsafe”?
No. cost-efficient is intended to be safe-by-default. It can, however, expose issues in client configuration more often (e.g., too-short timeouts) because it may add queueing under high load.

We also pair cost-efficient with overload protection so that under extreme load we prefer graceful degradation (backpressure / controlled shedding) rather than uncontrolled tail latency.

9) When should I override tier defaults (advanced tuning)?
Most customers should start with a tier and avoid overrides unless they have a clear need.

Consider overrides if:
- You have very low concurrency and still see higher latency than expected (batching won’t help much; queue delay may be unnecessary).
- You have extreme long-context prompts and are seeing memory pressure (KV cache) issues.
- You have unusual traffic patterns (microbursts) and want stricter queue delay caps.
- You need to align server batching with a fixed client timeout budget.

If you override, we recommend changing one thing at a time and watching queue delay + tail latency.

10) If I set a tier, can I still set explicit batching parameters?
Yes. Precedence rule (expected behavior):
- Explicit per-deployment or per-route batching settings override the tier defaults.
- Tier defaults fill in “missing” values.

This lets you keep the tier as a baseline while adjusting a specific knob.

11) How do I know what batching settings I’m actually running (“effective config”)?
You can validate tier behavior via:
- Console: view the selected tier and the computed defaults applied for that model + deployment.
- Observability: dashboards showing queue delay, batch size distribution, and latency percentiles by tier.
- API/config introspection: some environments expose an “explain effective config” view so you can see what the runtime is using after applying tier defaults + overrides.

If Support asks for “effective config,” include:
- tier
- any explicit batching overrides
- model name + version
- region
- deployment mode (Hosted / Dedicated / Private)

12) Do tiers apply to embeddings and reranking too?
Yes, but the trade-offs can look different:
- Embeddings are often throughput-oriented; cost-efficient can be a strong default.
- Reranking can be latency-sensitive depending on usage in search UI; standard or fast may be better for interactive search.

If an embeddings workload is user-facing (e.g., on-the-fly query embeddings), treat it like interactive and consider fast/standard.

13) Will tiers behave the same across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private?
The tier names and intent are consistent across Hosted / Dedicated / Private.
Actual performance depends on:
- hardware SKU
- autoscaling and capacity headroom
- model family and context lengths
- your request mix (prompt length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming)

Dedicated and Private deployments may also have more control over concurrency limits and autoscaling, which influences how well each tier performs.

14) What if I try cost-efficient and see more timeouts?
Common causes:
- Client-side timeout too low for the new queue delay under peak load
- Retries amplifying load (retry storm)
- Requests competing with other traffic on shared capacity (Hosted)

Recommended steps:
1) Switch back to standard (or fast if streaming UX is critical) to confirm the issue is tier-related.
2) Check queue delay and p95/p99 latency dashboards for that route/model.
3) Check cancellation/timeout rate and whether timeouts correlate with higher concurrency.
4) If you must stay on cost-efficient, consider:
   - raising client timeout (if acceptable)
   - setting a stricter max queue delay override
   - using per-route tiering (only apply cost-efficient where it’s safe)

(We have a Support playbook in progress; ask Support for the “Tiered batching troubleshooting checklist” if you need help.)

15) Can I choose different tiers per route or per request?
Supported patterns depend on your integration:
- Per route/deployment: recommended.
- Per request: may be supported in certain APIs/SDKs; use carefully because it can complicate capacity planning and makes performance harder to predict.

If you want different tiers per request, talk to your Solutions Engineer to ensure observability and guardrails are in place.

16) Does cost-efficient always reduce cost?
It usually reduces $/token under steady load because it increases GPU utilization via larger/more efficient batches.
Cases where cost-efficient may not help:
- very low traffic / low concurrency (not enough work to batch)
- extremely spiky traffic with tight timeouts (wasted work due to cancellations/timeouts)
- long-context workloads dominated by memory constraints (batching limited by KV cache)

17) How should I measure whether a tier is “working”?
We recommend watching:
- Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), especially TTFT for streaming
- Queue delay distribution
- Batch size distribution and batch formation rate
- GPU utilization / tokens-per-second
- Timeout and cancellation rates
- $/1M tokens (or your unit cost metric)

Compare before/after with the same traffic profile, and avoid comparing across different prompt length mixes.

18) What’s the default tier if I don’t choose one?
During beta, defaults may vary by model/region and may be gated behind a feature flag.
- If a default tier is applied automatically, it will be visible in Console/effective config.
- You can always explicitly set a tier to pin behavior.

TODO: confirm what we want to say for GA. Likely: “standard is the default unless you override.”

19) Example: How do I set a tier?
(Exact syntax depends on SDK/API; final docs will include copy/paste examples.)

Example (conceptual JSON config):
- batching_tier: "standard"

Example (conceptual): overriding one knob while still using a tier
- batching_tier: "cost_efficient"
- max_queue_delay_ms: 10   (override just this if you need a tighter cap)

20) I’m still not sure which tier to pick — what info should I provide to Redwood?
Send:
- model + version
- region(s)
- streaming vs non-streaming
- typical prompt length and output length (ranges are fine)
- concurrency / QPS patterns (steady vs bursty)
- your SLO (what matters most: TTFT, p95 end-to-end, token cadence)
- current timeout/retry policy
- whether this is Hosted / Dedicated / Private
